title: The Fog Lady of Marrowby Point
author: Edmund Hallowell Reyes

chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Bird in the Wall
paragraphs: The village of Marrowby sat at the end of a long, crooked road, and beyond it there was nothing but grey sea. On the last rock of the point stood the lighthouse, tall and white and slightly leaning, as if it were listening for something far out on the water. Nell Harrow had looked at it every morning of her twelve years, and she had never once thought it might not always be there. That changed on a wet Tuesday in early October, when a man in a yellow raincoat nailed a notice to the door of the village hall.

"What does it say?" asked Kofi Mensah, squinting through the drizzle. He was Nell's best friend, and he was shorter than she was by exactly one head, a fact he pretended not to notice. Nell read it aloud, slowly, because the words did not seem to want to be read. "By order of the Coastal Authority, the Marrowby Point light will be extinguished for the last time on the fourteenth of October. The tower will be sealed and offered for sale." She stopped. "Sealed. They are going to seal it, Kofi." "But the ships," he said.

Nell lived with her grandfather in the narrow house above the harbour, where the front room smelled of oil and brass and old tea. Tobias Harrow had mended clocks for fifty-one years, and his workbench was covered in tiny wheels, tweezers, and glass domes that ticked gently like a sleeping crowd. He looked up when she came in, and he knew at once. "You have seen the notice," he said. "It's not fair, Grandpa."

He did not, in fact, have anything. What he had was a request. The lighthouse keeper's cottage, empty for years, was being cleared before the sale, and the council clerk, a stiff and careful man named Mr. Pettigrew, had asked whether the town clockmaker might look at the old clock in the lamp room before it was carted away. Tobias was too old for the spiral stairs. Nell was not. "Would you go for me?" he asked. "Tomorrow, after school. Take your small toolbox. And take Kofi, if his mother allows it. Nobody should climb that tower alone."

She did not need to be asked twice. The next afternoon the two of them stood at the foot of the lighthouse, looking up. The door was green, the paint peeling in long curls. Mr. Pettigrew was waiting with a ring of heavy keys and a clipboard, which he held against his chest like a shield.

"One hundred and forty-two steps," he said, turning the lock. "I counted them once. Do not touch the lamp, do not lean on the rail, and be down by half past five. The light will be on a timer, and I do not want anyone near it when it wakes."

At the top, the lamp room was a round glass cage full of grey light. The great lens stood in the middle, taller than Kofi, its rings of glass glittering like frozen water. In the corner, on a bracket, hung the clock: a fat brass thing with a cracked face and a pendulum that had long since stopped.

Nell opened her toolbox and set to work. It took her twenty minutes to find the problem, and when she did, she found something else as well. Behind the clock, the plaster of the wall had crumbled away in a patch the size of a dinner plate, and inside the hollow, wrapped in a scrap of oilcloth, something small was glinting. "Kofi," she whispered. "Come and look at this."

chapters.title: Chapter 2: A Key Shaped Like a Feather
paragraphs: It was a bird. Nell lifted it out of the oilcloth with both hands, the way she would have lifted a real one, and it lay in her palms, heavy and cool. A gull, no longer than her forearm, made entirely of brass and tarnished silver. Its wings were folded tight. Its eyes were two small chips of blue glass, and in its back, between the shoulders, was a tiny round keyhole. "It is a toy," Kofi said.

"It is not a toy." She turned it over. The feathers were etched one by one, each barely thicker than a hair, and the joints at the wings moved with a smoothness that no toy would ever have. "Somebody spent months on this. Maybe years."

Underneath the bird, folded into the oilcloth, lay a single sheet of paper gone brown at the edges. The handwriting was small and upright. Nell read it by the window, tilting it toward the light. "To whoever finds her after me. Her name is Margaret. She was made to sing when the fog comes, and she will do so only if wound with the key I have hidden where the light is brightest. Be gentle with her. She is the last honest thing I made. Captain L. Quince, keeper, October 1894." "October 1894," Kofi said slowly. "That is one hundred and thirty years ago."

"Almost exactly. And look, there is more." On the back, in a different, hurried hand, someone had added a line. "The town must never lose the light. Tell them the paper is in the keel." "What paper? What keel?" Kofi scratched his head. "There is no boat in a lighthouse."

"I don't know." Nell folded the sheet carefully and slid it into her pocket. Then she looked at the great lens, glittering a few paces away, and a strange idea came to her. "The key is hidden where the light is brightest. Kofi, where is the light brightest?" He followed her gaze. "Inside the lens. At the very centre. But we are not allowed to touch it." "We are not allowed to touch the lamp," she said. "Mr. Pettigrew said so. He said nothing about looking."

They crouched on the iron floor and peered through the lowest ring of glass. At the centre, where the bulb sat in its cradle, a ring of brass held everything in place. And on that ring, just where the old flame had once burned, a small shape was fixed with a dab of wax. It was a key, flat and curved, with its handle cut in the shape of a feather. "Half past five," Kofi reminded her, glancing at the window. The sky had darkened to the colour of slate. "And the fog is coming in."

"Then she will sing tonight," Nell said, "if we can wake her." "I know." She wrapped the gull in her scarf and tucked it inside her jacket, against her chest, where she could feel its small weight like a second heartbeat. "We will tell my grandfather. He will know what to do about the key." Mr. Pettigrew was waiting at the bottom, tapping his watch. "Twenty-eight minutes past," he said, with some satisfaction. "Cutting it fine. Did you fix the clock?"

"Good. Good. I shall expect it finished by Friday." He locked the green door behind them and dropped the keys into his pocket. Then he stopped, and for a moment his stiff face changed. He looked up at the tower, and his voice came out smaller than before. "My father kept the light for eleven years, you know. Before the machines. I used to sit on those steps and do my homework."

At the clockmaker's house, when she had told him everything, her grandfather laughed, very quietly, and wiped his eyes with the back of his hand. "Margaret," he said. "Well, I never. I have heard that name since I was a boy."

chapters.title: Chapter 3: What Grandpa Remembered
paragraphs: Tobias lowered himself into his armchair and stirred his tea three times, which was what he always did before telling a story. Kofi sat cross-legged on the rug. Nell perched on the arm of the sofa with the gull in her lap, and outside the window the fog pressed its white face against the glass.

"My grandmother used to tell it," he began. "She was a girl in the great fog of 1921. For three days the whole coast vanished. No light could be seen, no horn could be heard, and eleven fishing boats were out beyond the point with nothing to steer by."

"Eleven. Their families stood on the sea wall all night, calling into the white. And then, my grandmother said, something began to sing. Not a bell, not a horn. A clear, high, sweet sound, like a flute made of glass. It came from the top of the lighthouse, and it rose and fell in a pattern the fishermen knew by heart, because they had heard it every foggy night of their childhoods. They steered toward it. By dawn, all eleven boats had come home." Nell looked down at the gull. "Margaret."

"The village called her the Fog Lady. Nobody ever saw her, you understand. People said it was a pipe organ, or a trick of the wind in the vents. The keeper at the time was a gruff old fellow who refused to talk about it." Tobias took a long sip of tea. "Then, sometime before the war, the singing stopped. The key was lost, they said, or the mechanism seized. In a few years, people forgot there had ever been a sound at all."

"Except my grandmother, and then me." He smiled. "I never believed it, to be honest. I thought it was a tale for children. And all this time she was sitting behind a clock, forty paces from where I used to play." Tobias rubbed his chin, and a hundred clocks ticked, and at the very moment the old cuckoo on the wall began to announce seven o'clock, someone knocked at the front door.

It was a woman in a long green coat, carrying a leather case. She had silver hair cut short, sharp grey eyes, and a smile that arrived a little too quickly. Rain glittered on her shoulders. "Mr. Harrow? Forgive me for calling so late. I am Dr. Imelda Voss, from the county museum. Mr. Pettigrew mentioned that your granddaughter had made a remarkable discovery this afternoon." Nell's hand tightened on the gull. She had told no one but Tobias and Kofi, and Mr. Pettigrew had not seen the bird at all.

"He did not, exactly." Dr. Voss's eyes rested for a moment on the bundle in Nell's lap, and the smile did not waver. "He said you had been asking about the plaster behind the old clock. I have spent twenty years studying the automata of the Victorian lighthouse service, my dear. When a child is seen carrying a scarf-wrapped parcel out of a tower of that age, one does not need to be a genius."

"Thank you, but I shall not stay," said Dr. Voss. She set her case on the table and opened it. Inside, nested in grey foam, was a velvet-lined space exactly the size of the gull. "I have come to make an offer. The museum would be honoured to house this piece. We can pay two thousand five hundred pounds, today, in full." "Two thousand five hundred," said Tobias at last, and his voice was very gentle. "That is a great deal of money." "It is a great deal of money," agreed Dr. Voss. "And she will be safe, I promise you. Dry, warm, and admired."
Nell looked at her grandfather, and he looked at her, and between them passed something that did not need words.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: An Offer Declined
paragraphs: "We cannot sell her tonight," Nell said. Her voice came out steadier than she expected. "She is not finished. She has not sung yet." Dr. Voss tilted her head. "Singing is a lovely thought, my dear, but a mechanism that has been silent for a century is rarely worth the effort of waking. Spring steel fatigues. Leather perishes. If you wind her carelessly, she will break."

"I am sure he will not." The doctor turned to Tobias, and her tone grew warmer, almost confiding. "Mr. Harrow, you are a craftsman. You understand. A piece like this belongs where specialists can study it, with proper temperature controls, proper records. Here, she is one rainy night away from a leaking ceiling."

"I know what you mean, Doctor. And you may well be right." He folded his hands. "But the bird was found in a tower that belongs, for another few weeks, to the people of this village, and it was found by a girl of twelve who climbed one hundred and forty-two steps to mend a clock for nothing. I would not feel easy selling her before the girl has had her say. And she has had it."

Dr. Voss looked at Nell for a long moment. Then she closed her case with two neat clicks. "The offer will stand until the fourteenth," she said. "After that date the tower is sealed, and I fear the Authority will claim everything inside it as its own property. Including, I should think, whatever is hidden behind its walls. You may find it simpler to be paid now." She left a cream-coloured card on the table. The door shut behind her, and the fog swallowed the sound of her footsteps.

Nell took out the paper and read it carefully. "The town must never lose the light. Tell them the paper is in the keel." "The keel," her grandfather repeated, and then something flickered across his face, a spark of memory struck like a match. "Kofi, does your father still keep the upturned boat behind the net shed?" "The old Marigold? Yes, Mr. Harrow. He uses her for storing crab pots. Nobody has sailed her for years."

"She was built in 1890," said Tobias, "in the village yard, by the same men who put up the lighthouse. My grandmother told me they used timber left over from the tower scaffolding. And a keel, my dears, is a very good place to hide a paper."

"Tomorrow, by all means," said Tobias, "but not at dawn, and not with a crowbar. Marigold has survived a hundred and thirty-four years. She does not deserve to be taken apart by two excited children." They ate a late supper of cheese and pickle sandwiches, and Kofi was sent home with a torch and a stern promise to be at the shed by a quarter to eight. When he had gone, Nell sat on the bottom stair for a long time, looking at the card Dr. Voss had left. Under the museum's crest, in elegant type, it read: Imelda Voss, Ph.D., Keeper of Mechanical Antiquities.

"Keeper," she said to herself. "She calls herself a keeper too." Upstairs, she lay awake listening to the foghorn from the ferry, a low, flat bellow that rolled across the harbour and died away. It was not a beautiful sound. It said only, I am here, keep away. She thought of the sweet glass flute that had once guided eleven boats safely home, and she wondered whether anyone had ever been sorry to lose it.

Sometime after midnight, the fog thinned, and a single star came out above the point. It shone on the dark tower, and on the boat behind the net shed, and on a small brass gull lying wrapped in a scarf beside a sleeping girl's bed.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Marigold
paragraphs: The net shed stood at the far end of the harbour, a long low building the colour of driftwood. Behind it, propped on rotting trestles and half buried in nets and lobster pots, lay the Marigold, upside down like a sleeping whale. Her paint had faded from blue to the pale grey of an old bruise, but her ribs were still straight and strong. Kofi was already there, holding his father's biggest torch and a ruler.

They cleared the pots one by one, stacking them in a careful tower beside the shed wall. Then they crawled underneath the hull, into a world of damp wood and spider silk and green-gold light leaking through the cracks in the planks. The keel ran down the middle of the boat like a spine, a single massive beam of oak, black with age.

Nell ran her fingers along it from bow to stern. She felt carved initials, a rusted bolt, a smear of tar. Nothing else. Then, near the stern, her thumb caught on something that was not quite wood: a thin line, perfectly straight, running across the grain. "Kofi, shine the torch here."

It was a seam. Someone had cut a narrow slot into the underside of the keel, a hand's width long, and sealed it with a plug of wood so carefully fitted that it had almost vanished into the surrounding grain. The tar had been painted over it a century ago, and over that, a dozen later coats.

"A ruler will do." She slid the thin edge into the seam and worked it slowly back and forth. Dust fell onto her face. The plug resisted, and then gave a small wooden groan and slid out into her palm. Inside the slot, wrapped in layers of waxed cloth, lay a flat tin box about the size of a book.

They did not open it under the boat. They carried it between them, as solemnly as pallbearers, across the harbour and up the hill to the clockmaker's house, where Tobias was waiting with a pot of tea and an expression of enormous restraint. School, for that morning at least, was entirely forgotten.

The tin lid was rusted shut. It took Tobias twenty minutes, a drop of oil, and a thin steel blade to coax it open. Inside, folded in three, lay a large sheet of heavy paper. It was brittle and stained, but the writing on it was bold, and at the bottom there were nearly two hundred signatures, some careful, some scrawled, some no more than crosses with a name written beside them by someone else. Tobias put on his glasses and began to read aloud.

"We the undersigned, being fishermen, farmers, shopkeepers, and widows of the parish of Marrowby, do hereby subscribe the sum of one shilling and upward toward the building of a lighthouse upon Marrowby Point. And we do declare that the said lighthouse shall be held in trust for the people of this parish, and shall not be sold, closed, or put to any other use without the consent of a majority of their number, assembled in open meeting."

"Dated the ninth of March, 1893. Witnessed by the Reverend A. Thorne and by Lowell Quince, appointed keeper." He lowered the paper and looked at them over his glasses. "Children, this is not a diary or a love letter. This is a deed. The people of Marrowby built that tower with their own pennies, and they wrote down, in plain ink, that nobody could take it away without asking them first."

Nell sat very still. In her mind she saw the green door, and Mr. Pettigrew's stiff shoulders, and all the little ordinary faces of the village that she had known since birth. Two hundred signatures, she thought. Each of them had once stood in a cold church hall and decided that the sea was not going to be left alone in the dark.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Mr. Pettigrew Is Not Convinced
paragraphs: "It is a very interesting document," said Mr. Pettigrew. He sat behind the desk in the council office with the old deed spread out before him under a sheet of clear plastic, and he had not blinked in nearly a minute. The office was a small, tidy room above the post office, and it smelled of floor polish and paper. On the wall hung a framed photograph of the lighthouse in better days, its lamp blazing white against a stormy sky.

"It is a very interesting document, and I should be delighted to forward it to the Authority's legal department. They will examine it. They will compare the signatures with parish records. It will take, I imagine, between four and six months." "The light goes out on the fourteenth of October!" Kofi burst out. "That is in ten days."

"Quite so." Mr. Pettigrew straightened his tie. "Which is why I must be careful. Young man, a clerk cannot halt an order from the Coastal Authority on the strength of a paper found in a boat. If the deed turns out to be a forgery, or a draft that was never ratified, I will have wasted the council's time and made the village look foolish. Do you understand?"

"I know the handwriting matches the note by Captain Quince. I know the boat was built in 1890, three years before the deed. I know the tin box was sealed inside the keel with tar that has been there for a century." She felt her face grow hot. "Mr. Pettigrew, you told us your father kept the light for eleven years. You told us you used to do your homework on those steps."
For the first time, the clerk's composure slipped. He took off his glasses and pinched the bridge of his nose. When he spoke again, it was without the official voice.

"My father cried on the last night he worked there," he said. "He was forty-nine. He sat on the bottom step with his cap in his hands, and I did not know what to say to him. I was a boy, you see. I thought grown men did not cry." He put his glasses back on. "I have been a clerk for twenty-six years, Nell. I follow the rules because the rules are the only thing that stops everything falling to bits. But I do not enjoy this notice. I never have."

"I will do what I properly can." He drew a sheet of letterhead toward him and uncapped a pen. "Under the parish charter, a public meeting may be called on seven days' notice if fifty residents sign a request. If there is a meeting, and if the villagers vote, and if this deed is found to be genuine, then the Authority's order may be challenged. That is a great many ifs. But they are not impossible ifs."

"I shall have the request ready by noon tomorrow." Mr. Pettigrew hesitated, and a faint pink crept up his neck. "There is one more difficulty. The lens door can be opened only with the master set of keys that I carry, and I cannot allow anyone to open it without authority."

"There is one more thing," said Nell. "The bird has a key, and the note says it is hidden inside the lens. We are not asking you to break any rules. Only for permission to wake her once, on a foggy night, before the light goes out, so that the village can hear what the Fog Lady sounds like."

Mr. Pettigrew was silent for a very long time. Outside, a gull shrieked, and a delivery van rattled past on the cobbles. Finally he took out the ring of heavy keys, turned one over in his fingers, and put it back. "The forecast," he said carefully, "predicts fog on Saturday evening. At about eight o'clock. I could imagine being at the lighthouse at that time, to check the timer. I could imagine, purely by accident, leaving the lens door unlocked." Nell grinned so widely it hurt.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: The Fog Lady Wakes
paragraphs: Saturday came in grey and still. By lunchtime the sea had gone flat as pewter, and the air tasted of salt and cold iron. Tobias stood at the kitchen window with his hands clasped behind his back and sniffed, like a dog reading a message.

At half past seven, wrapped in two scarves and a woollen hat, Nell walked up the point with her grandfather leaning on her arm and Kofi trotting ahead with the torch. The fog was thickening. It rose from the water in slow white curls, and behind them the village lights shrank to a smudge and then went out altogether, one by one, like candles in a cathedral.

Mr. Pettigrew stood by the green door, his clipboard under his arm. He had not worn his usual tie. "I have, ah, checked the timer," he said, to no one in particular. "It appears to be functioning. The lens door appears to be... unlatched. I shall wait down here and make a note of any irregularities."

Tobias could not manage the whole climb, so they went slowly, with a rest at every twentieth step. When they reached the top, he sat down on the iron floor with his back against the wall and waved a hand. "Go on. I shall be here when you are done, and I shall be perfectly happy to listen."

The lens door stood ajar. Nell pushed it open, and the great glass rings sighed softly as they moved. Inside, she could see the brass cradle and the dab of wax and the little feather-shaped key, shining in the lamp room's last grey light. She reached up on tiptoe, her fingertips just brushing the cold metal, and eased the key loose. It came away in her hand with a faint click.

She held the key up. It was warm, which was impossible, and she decided it must be her own hand. Then she took the gull from her pocket, turned it over, and slid the key into the keyhole between the shoulders. It fitted as though they had never been parted.

She turned. One half turn, then another. Somewhere inside the brass, a spring caught, and a tiny wheel began to tick. A whisper of air slid through the gull's chest. Nell put her on the window ledge, facing out into the dark, and stepped back. Then the gull lifted her head.

It was only a small movement, a tilt of the neck, but it was so lifelike that Nell's breath stopped. The blue glass eyes caught the faint light. The wings opened, a quarter of an inch, and the beak parted, and out of the little brass throat came a note.

It was the clearest sound she had ever heard. It was a flute and a bell and a child's voice all at once, high and sweet and impossibly pure, and it did not so much fill the room as pass through it, like light through water. It rose, held, fell, and rose again in a pattern of three long notes and two short, over and over, until the whole lamp room seemed to hum with it.

"That is it," he said hoarsely. "That is exactly what my grandmother described. Three long, two short." He laughed unsteadily. "Hello, Margaret. We have been waiting for you for a very long time." The song drifted out of the open vent, over the rail, and down into the fog. Nell ran to the window and pressed her forehead to the glass. Out there in the whiteness, small and far away, a light blinked on. Then another. Windows were opening all along the harbour road, and people were stepping out of their doors in their slippers, with their faces turned toward the tower.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: The Whole Village Listens
paragraphs: By the time Nell, Kofi, and Tobias came down the spiral stairs, a crowd had gathered at the foot of the tower. They had come in coats thrown over pyjamas, in fishing boots, in aprons dusted with flour. Kofi's mother was there, holding a baby on her hip, and so was the baker, and the retired schoolteacher from the corner house, and old Mrs. Ellery, who was ninety-three and had been carried up the hill on a kitchen chair by her two grandsons.

"It is her," Mrs. Ellery said, in a voice that cracked and shook. "I heard her when I was four years old. My father held me up to the window. I never told anyone, because they said I had dreamed it." She wiped her face with a lace handkerchief. "I did not dream it. Look at all of you. I did not dream it."

Nobody laughed at her. A man near the front, a big sunburnt fisherman called Davy Corrigan, took off his cap and stood bareheaded in the damp, and one by one the others did the same. At nine o'clock exactly the spring ran down, and the song wound to a gentle close, three long notes and two short, then silence. The crowd stood motionless for several breaths, as though afraid to disturb the quiet. Then Davy Corrigan began to clap, slow and heavy, and in a moment everyone was clapping, until the applause rolled out over the harbour and the fog swallowed it whole.

Tobias climbed down the last step and found himself surrounded. People were seizing his hands. "Is it true?" someone asked. "Was it in the wall the whole time?" "Can she sing again?" "Can she sing tomorrow?" "She can sing every foggy night, if she is wound," he said, raising his voice above the clamour. "But I should tell you something, all of you, and I should tell you now. After the fourteenth, there will be no light in that tower, and no keeper. The lens will be locked. The door will be sealed. And Margaret, I am afraid, will be sealed with it."

"Unless," said Nell. Every head turned. She had not meant to speak so loudly, and for a second her courage almost failed. Then she saw Kofi's face, nodding at her fiercely, and Mr. Pettigrew's, grave and attentive, and she took a breath.

"Unless you vote," she said. "We found a paper in the keel of the old Marigold. It was signed by two hundred people in 1893. Some of them might have been your great-grandparents. It says the lighthouse belongs to the village, and that it cannot be closed or sold unless the village agrees." She swallowed. "Mr. Pettigrew says there can be a public meeting if fifty people sign. It will be in the village hall on Friday at half past seven. All we have to do is come."

For a heartbeat there was no sound but the dripping of the fog. Then Mrs. Ellery lifted a thin hand from the arm of her kitchen chair. "I shall sign," she said. "Though I may need someone to hold the pen." Laughter broke out, warm and ragged, and then suddenly everyone was talking at once, planning and arguing and promising. Nell stood in the middle of it with her hands pressed over her mouth, feeling as though the ground had tilted gently beneath her feet. She felt Kofi's elbow dig into her ribs.

But beyond the heads of the crowd, at the edge of the lantern light, she noticed a figure in a long green coat watching in silence. Dr. Voss did not wave, and she did not smile. She simply stood there a moment longer, and then turned and walked away into the white.

chapters.title: Chapter 9: The Meeting in the Hall
paragraphs: On Friday evening, the village hall was so full that people sat on the window sills and stood three deep along the back wall. The tea urn hissed in the corner. Someone had dragged the old piano against the door to make more room, and a row of children sat cross-legged at the front, swinging their feet.

Three officials from the Coastal Authority sat behind a long table on the stage. The one in the middle, a tall woman named Ms. Okafor, wore a navy suit and the patient expression of someone who has attended many angry meetings. Beside her sat Mr. Pettigrew, pale but upright, and at the far end, to Nell's surprise, sat Dr. Voss, with her leather case on her knees. "I call this meeting to order," said Ms. Okafor, tapping a small wooden gavel. "I understand there is a document to be considered. Mr. Pettigrew?"

"The Authority has examined a photograph of this paper," said Ms. Okafor. "I will be frank. If it is genuine, it complicates matters considerably. Dr. Voss, I understand you have expertise in the period." "I do," the doctor said. "I have spent four days examining the ink, the paper, and the signatures, comparing them with the parish registers at the county archive. I am bound to tell this meeting that the document is genuine."

"I am also bound to tell you," she continued, "that when I first came to this village, I did so for a selfish reason. I had heard rumours of a Victorian automaton, and I wished to acquire it for my museum. I offered the family who found it two thousand five hundred pounds." She looked down the hall, directly at Nell. "I now believe that was a mistake. On Saturday night I stood in the fog and listened to that machine sing. And I realised that twenty years of collecting had taught me nothing about what an object is for."

"A thing in a case is a fact," said Dr. Voss. "A thing that does its work is a gift. I would be proud to see that bird remain exactly where she was meant to be, and I will say so in writing to the Authority." The applause came slowly and then all at once. Ms. Okafor let it run for a long moment before she rapped the gavel again.

"The deed may be genuine," she said, "but the Authority still has practical concerns. The tower needs repairs, and the roof leaks. The lamp is old and costly to run. The sum required is estimated at forty-eight thousand pounds. If the village wishes to retain the lighthouse, it must show that it can maintain it." The hall went very quiet. Forty-eight thousand pounds was more than the whole village had in its savings. Then, at the back, a chair scraped. Mrs. Ellery was standing, supported by both grandsons, her thin voice carrying surprisingly far.

"My dear," Mrs. Ellery said, her thin voice carrying surprisingly far, "my grandmother gave a shilling in 1893 and her grandson wrote it in a family Bible. We are not a rich village. But we have never needed to be rich. We have needed only to be asked."

Nell had not planned to speak. She heard her own voice before she knew she had stood. "Please, may I say something? Margaret does not just sing. She is a bell for the fog. People pay to see old things in museums. They would pay to come here, too, to hear her. A visitor tour, a tea room in the keeper's cottage, a small museum in the lamp room. Dr. Voss could advise, and Mr. Pettigrew could keep the accounts, and..." "And I could mend the clock," said Tobias, from the front row.

Everybody laughed, and the sound loosened something in the hall. Hands began to rise: the baker, the schoolteacher, Davy Corrigan, forty hands, then eighty. Ms. Okafor looked at them for a very long time, and then she picked up her pen.

chapters.title: Chapter 10: The Light Stays On
paragraphs: The vote was carried by two hundred and six hands to nine. Ms. Okafor read the result twice, as though checking that she had not misheard, and then wrote a note in the margin of her papers that Nell could not read from where she sat. Afterward, over tea and ginger biscuits, the Authority agreed to a trial period of three years. The village would run the lighthouse as a trust, just as the deed had always said it should, and the Authority would continue to fund the lamp for the first twelve months.

"It is not a victory," Ms. Okafor told Nell, bending so that their eyes were level. "Not yet. It is a promise to try. But I have been to a great many meetings, and I have never been to one where an old lady offered to hold a pen for a whole village." She shook Nell's hand. "Look after her, will you?" "Which her?" asked Nell. "The bird or the lighthouse?" "Yes," said Ms. Okafor.

By the middle of December they had raised eleven thousand pounds. It was a long way from forty-eight thousand. But Dr. Voss, true to her word, wrote a letter to a heritage foundation, and in January an envelope arrived with a cheque for thirty-eight thousand more, and a handwritten line at the bottom from someone who had once been told by a clock that the world could still be surprising.

On the first Saturday of March, the Marrowby Point Lighthouse opened its doors to visitors for the first time in forty years. A hand-painted sign hung above the green door, freshly repainted, and under it, on a stand, stood a small brass gull in a glass case that was not locked. Nell had insisted on that. "She should be touched," she said, "gently, by people who understand."

The first visitor was a boy of about six, holding his mother's hand. He stared up at the great lens, and at the gull, and at Tobias, who was sitting on a stool beside the clock with his tweezers in his hand, and he said, very clearly, "Is she alive?" "That depends what you mean," said Tobias. "She sings only in the fog. Come back on a misty evening, and bring your mother."

Late that afternoon, when the last visitor had gone and the sun was sinking red over the water, Nell and Kofi climbed the one hundred and forty-two steps alone. They sat on the iron floor of the lamp room with their backs against the cold wall and their legs stretched out in front of them, and for a long time they said nothing at all. "Do you think Captain Quince would be pleased?" Kofi asked finally.

"I think he knew," Nell said. "I think he hid her and the deed because he trusted us to find them. Not us exactly. Someone. Whoever would be standing here when it mattered." "It is what the whole light was for, though, isn't it?" She tucked her knees under her chin. "Someone out in the dark, trusting that someone else is awake."

Far out on the horizon, a line of pale mist was beginning to creep over the water, soft as breath on a window. Nell watched it for a minute and then smiled to herself. She got up, took the little feather-shaped key from the hook where they now kept it, and walked to the case. "Wind her?" asked Kofi. "Just this once," she said. "For practice." Three long notes rose into the dusk, and two short, and far below, the first lamps came on in the village of Marrowby, one by one, to listen.
